t: Minimum Cost to Make All Characters Equal — Boundary Greedy
o: We must make a binary string uniform using prefix flips (cost i+1) or suffix flips (cost n-i). Walk through "0011": flipping the suffix starting at index 2 (cost 2) fixes everything, matching the expected output 2. For "010101" every adjacent pair differs, and picking the cheaper side at each boundary yields 1+2+3+2+1=9. The key observation: consider each adjacent pair (i, i+1) independently. If s[i] == s[i+1] they end equal under any global plan without wasted work; if they differ, exactly one 'boundary' must be crossed by an operation, and the cheapest crossing is min(i+1, n-i-1). With n up to 1e5 we need an O(n) pass, ruling out any exponential search over operation sequences.
k: Only adjacent unequal pairs matter; each such boundary must be paid for exactly once.
The cheapest way to 'cut' boundary i is min(i+1, n-i-1) — flip the shorter side.
Summing these minima over all differing boundaries gives the optimal answer.

a.i: Each mismatched adjacent pair forces one flip whose range crosses that boundary. A prefix flip of cost i+1 and a suffix flip of cost n-i-1 both cross it, and doing more than one flip per boundary is never beneficial (flips would cancel or overshoot). So the answer is the sum of the per-boundary minimums.
s: If s[i] != s[i+1], add min(i+1, n-i-1) to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over adjacent pairs.

a.i: Simulate decisions boundary by boundary while tracking a parity flag 'suf' = whether past suffix flips have inverted every character seen so far. When the (parity-adjusted) neighbors differ, pay the cheaper side; choosing the suffix flip toggles 'suf' because it affects all characters to the right. Prefix flips never affect future comparisons, so they need no state.
s: For each boundary i, compare s[i] XOR suf with s[i+1] XOR suf.
On mismatch add min(i+1, n-i-1); if the suffix side was cheaper, toggle suf.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per boundary.
a.sp: O(1) — a flag and an accumulator.

w: Use Approach 1 in an interview — it is shorter and the independence argument is easy to defend. Pitfalls: forgetting the boundary at i = n-2 uses cost n-i-1 = 1, and using int overflow is not an issue here but returning long long in C++/Java matches the signature. Follow-ups: what if flip costs were arbitrary arrays, or if you could flip any subrange for its length?
